evidence.label: Arithmeticity of twisted finite correspondences for lattices over local fields
The arithmetic category and stable recovery of lattice factors

headline: Claims the von Neumann algebra of a property (T) lattice remembers its group, its twist and its scale.
scope: Scalar-twisted group factors of ICC groups commensurable with property (T) lattices over characteristic-zero local fields, compared with any countable ICC group.
plain: From any group one can build an operator algebra called its group factor. A long-standing question asks how much of the group survives in that algebra. Two companion papers study groups like SL₃(ℤ), integer 3-by-3 matrices of determinant 1, and their relatives. They claim every finite-index link between such a factor and another group factor comes from actual subgroup matches. From this they claim the factor recovers the group, its twist and its scale.
doesNot: This does not cover every property (T) group, and other papers show property (T) alone does not ensure recovery.
origin: This result comes from an unreleased OpenAI model, published in the openai/math release on 6 October 2026.

scorecard.firstStepBy: Alain Connes, countability of the fundamental group of a property (T) group factor
scorecard.significanceWhy: It gives stable recovery of the group from its factor for a broad class of lattices, answering Connes- and Popa-type rigidity questions there.

explanation:
Take the group SL₃(ℤ), all 3-by-3 integer matrices with determinant 1. Reduce each entry modulo 2. You get a map onto the 3-by-3 matrices over the two-element field with determinant 1. That finite group has (8 − 1)(8 − 2)(8 − 4) = 7 × 6 × 4 = 168 elements. The matrices that map to the identity form a subgroup of index 168. Index counts how many copies of the subgroup fill the whole group.

From a group one can build an operator algebra, its group factor. Each group element becomes a unitary operator, and the algebra is their closure. A scalar twist multiplies products by fixed complex numbers of size one. The question is how much of the group the factor remembers. Connes proved that the fundamental group of a property (T) group factor is countable[1]. That fundamental group lists the scales t at which the factor matches its own resized copy. Property (T) is a strong rigidity condition on unitary representations. But property (T) alone does not ensure recovery. OpenAI and Zhou independently built different property (T) groups with the same group factor[2]. The obstacle is that the comparison group can be any group, with no geometry to start from.

The papers work with a looser link called a bifinite correspondence. It is a space where both factors act, with finite size on each side. The subgroup above gives one. Match it to itself and use a one-dimensional representation. The formula then gives size n × 168 on each side, with n = 1, so 168[3]. The first paper claims every bifinite correspondence is built from such models[4]. These come from real finite-index subgroup isomorphisms and finite-dimensional projective representations. A nonzero correspondence forces the two groups to be commensurable, sharing isomorphic finite-index subgroups[5].

The class is broad. It covers groups commensurable with lattices in products of simple groups over the real numbers, the complex numbers or p-adic fields. Lattices are discrete subgroups of finite covolume. SL₃(ℤ) and every finite-index subgroup belong to it[6]. The second paper claims stable recovery. Two resized twisted factors match only when the scales agree and the groups are isomorphic, with matching twists[7]. Every factor in the class has trivial fundamental group[8].

How sure is this? A computer proof checker called Lean has not checked any part of it. The argument builds geometry inside the correspondence over many long sections, including rank-one quaternionic and Cayley cases. No specialist review of the papers has been published.
hypeCheck: Major if it holds, for a wide class of lattices. It does not cover all property (T) groups, and it has no Lean check or published specialist review.

glossary.meaning: The operator algebra made by turning each group element into a unitary operator and closing up; a factor has trivial centre.
Infinite conjugacy classes: every element other than the identity has infinitely many conjugates.
A rigidity condition: any unitary representation with almost-invariant vectors has a truly invariant vector.
Two groups are commensurable if they have isomorphic subgroups of finite index.
A Hilbert space on which one factor acts from the left and another from the right, with finite size on both sides.
A rule assigning a complex number of size one to each pair of elements, used to twist multiplication.
The set of scales t at which the factor is isomorphic to its own resized copy.
A map to matrices that respects multiplication up to fixed scalar factors.

claims.text: If n is the dimension of the representation, the elementary model has dimensions n[Λ:B] and n[Γ:A].
claims.sourceQuote: If $n=\dim_{\mathbb C}V_\sigma$, the elementary model has dimensions \[ \dim_{L_\mu(\Gamma)}E(A,B,\delta,\sigma)=n[\Lambda:B],\qquad \dim E(A,B,\delta,\sigma)_{L_\omega(\Lambda)}=n[\Gamma:A]. \]

claims.text: Every bifinite correspondence is a closed summand of a finite direct sum of models from finite-index subgroup isomorphisms and finite-dimensional projective representations.
claims.sourceLine: Every bifinite $L_\mu(\Gamma)$--$L_\omega(\Lambda)$ correspondence is unitarily isomorphic to a closed bimodule summand of a finite direct sum
claims.sourceQuote: Every bifinite $L_\mu(\Gamma)$--$L_\omega(\Lambda)$ correspondence is unitarily isomorphic to a closed bimodule summand of a finite direct sum of the models $E(A,B,\delta,\sigma)$ in Equation~\eqref{eq:intro-model}, where $A\leq\Gamma$ and $B\leq\Lambda$ have finite index, $\delta:A\to B$ is an actual group isomorphism, and $\sigma$ is a finite-dimensional projective unitary representation satisfying Equation~\eqref{eq:intro-multiplier}.

claims.text: Amplified twisted factors are isomorphic if and only if the scales agree and the groups are isomorphic with cohomologous cocycles.
